title: Evaluating Statistical Claims, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: These questions describe a study and ask which conclusion the study supports. Two design features decide almost everything.

card.text: Which conclusion does the study support?

beats.say: The first is how the participants were selected, which controls whether you can generalize to a larger population. The second is whether treatments were randomly assigned, which controls whether you can claim cause and effect.
You also need to spot sampling bias, and compare results between groups.
Random selection from a population lets you generalize the results to that population, and only to that one.
Random assignment of treatments in an experiment lets you conclude cause and effect, because the groups differ only by chance.
An observational study, with no assigned treatment, can show an association, but never causation. People who choose a behavior may differ in other ways.
Sampling bias happens when the method favors certain people, such as volunteers, visitors to one website, customers at one store, or only those who are easy to reach.
The strongest claims are usually wrong. The best answer on the SAT is often the most modest one. Wording like proves, all, or will is a red flag.
If participants were randomly selected and treatments were randomly assigned, you can conclude cause and effect for the whole population that was sampled.
If participants were randomly selected, but there was no random assignment, you can only claim an association, but it applies to the population.
If participants weren't randomly selected, but treatments were randomly assigned, you can claim cause and effect, but only for the participants and people similar to them.
If neither was random, you can only claim an association, and only for the participants themselves.

Easy example. A researcher randomly selected three hundred members of a grocery chain's loyalty program, and found that sixty-two percent prefer evening hours. To which group can this result be generalized?

card.sub: 62% prefer evening hours. Generalize to whom?

beats.say: Question one. Who was selected, and how? The three hundred members were chosen at random, so the sample represents the group it was drawn from.
Question two. Which group was that? The sample was drawn from the loyalty program members of this chain, not from all shoppers, and not from all residents of the area.
So the result can be generalized to the members of this chain's loyalty program, and to no larger group. Any answer that mentions all shoppers or all residents goes too far.
To recap. Random selection decides who you can generalize to, and only to the group the sample was drawn from.
Random assignment decides whether you can claim cause and effect. Without it, you can only claim an association.
